businesses.name: White Duck Taco Shop
businesses.hook: What started as a food truck in a gas station parking lot is now an Asheville staple.
businesses.quote: We never set out to be a restaurant. We just wanted to make tacos people would drive across town for.
businesses.story:
Ben Mixson started White Duck Taco out of a converted bus in a gas station parking lot on the south side of Asheville. No business plan, no investors, just good tacos and word of mouth.

The lines got long enough that a brick-and-mortar became inevitable. Now there are multiple locations, but the vibe hasn't changed. The menu still rotates based on what's fresh and what sounds fun. You'll find Korean beef tacos next to jerk chicken next to a Thai peanut situation that has no business being that good.

Ben still shows up at the River Arts District location most mornings. He's less interested in scaling a brand and more interested in keeping the food worth talking about.

businesses.name: Blue Ridge Painting Co
businesses.hook: Three brothers who left corporate jobs to paint houses and haven't looked back.
businesses.quote: People think painting is simple. It is. But doing it right, on time, and without ghosting the client? That's where most guys fall apart.
businesses.story:
Jake, Matt, and Chris Harmon were all working desk jobs in Charlotte when their dad had a health scare in 2019. They moved back to Asheville to be closer to family and needed something to do.

Jake had painted houses in college. Matt could estimate and run numbers. Chris could sell. They pooled $5,000 and bought brushes, ladders, and a trailer. Blue Ridge Painting Co was born out of a garage in North Asheville.

Four years later, they run a crew of eight. Their reputation is built on one thing: they show up when they say they will. In an industry where ghosting is the norm, that alone has been enough to keep the phone ringing.

businesses.name: Second Gear
businesses.hook: Consignment outdoor gear for people who'd rather spend money on the trail than in the store.
businesses.quote: Everyone in Asheville has a garage full of gear they used twice. We give that gear a second life.
businesses.story:
Sarah Chen moved to Asheville for the mountains. She was spending her weekends on trails and her weekday paychecks at REI. When she noticed how many barely-used jackets, packs, and boots were collecting dust in friends' closets, the idea clicked.

Second Gear is a consignment shop on Haywood Road that buys and sells used outdoor gear. Patagonia jackets, hiking boots, climbing harnesses, camp stoves. If it belongs on a trail, it's probably on the rack.

The shop has become a hangout as much as a store. Trail runners swap route tips by the register. Weekend warriors try on packs. Sarah hosts free gear repair clinics on the first Saturday of every month.

businesses.name: Old Europe Pastries
businesses.hook: They almost closed in 2021. Now they run two kitchens until 10 PM.
businesses.quote: If we didn't find a new location, there would be no more Old Europe.
businesses.story:
Old Europe Pastries has been making downtown Asheville a little sweeter since 1994, when founder Melinda Vetro brought Hungarian baking techniques she'd learned in eighth grade to a city that had nothing quite like it. Thirty years and five locations later, the shop finally has a permanent home at 18 Broadway Street. Abigail Moore has been part of that story for eight of those years, first as a baker, now as GM, keeping the European-style cakes and tortes coming out the way Melinda always intended: lighter, less sweet, made the old way.

Getting there almost didn't happen. In 2021, in the middle of COVID, they got word they needed to find a new location or close for good. Abigail worked alongside Melinda through the property acquisition, the construction, and keeping the original location running at the same time. That's the version of determination most people never see from the outside of a pastry case.

Now they're running two full kitchens with 10 bakers working 7:30 AM to 10 PM. Ninety-five percent of what's in the case is made in-house, and no cake sits there longer than three days from baked layers to display. The hazelnut Napoleon is the bestseller, but the tiramisu, eclairs, and macarons move fast too. Thirty years of doing it right tends to have that effect.
